claims.source: The Vδ2 chain predominantly pairs with γ9 chain (LeFranc et al., 1986; Davey et al., 2018; Hinz et al., 1997) and these Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cells consist of up to 90% of the whole γδ T cell population in human peripheral blood (Wu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cells bear characteristics of innate immunity while Vγ9-Vδ2+ T cells have adaptive immune character.
claims.source: Although most studies do not discriminate between Vγ9+ and Vγ9- Vδ2 T cell subpopulations due to the scarcity of the latter, recent studies suggest that these cell subpopulations have distinct features: Vγ9+Vδ2+ bearing characteristics of innate immunity and Vγ9-Vδ2+ having adaptive immune character (Davey et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davey et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The antigens that activate Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cells comprise phosphoesters, alkylamines, nucleotide conjugates and heat shock proteins that are expressed by microbial pathogens but also by host cells.
claims.source: The antigens that activate Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cells comprise phosphoesters, alkylamines, nucleotide conjugates and heat shock proteins that are expressed by microbial pathogens but also by host cells (Fisch et al., 1979; Haregewoin et al., 1989; Bukowski et al., 1999; Constant et al., 1994; Tanaka et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fisch et al., 1979; Haregewoin et al., 1989; Bukowski et al., 1999; Constant et al., 1994; Tanaka et al., 1995.

claims.claim: The Vγ9+Vδ2+ TCR recognizes phosphoantigens such as HMB-PP and IPP.
claims.source: In particular, the Vγ9+Vδ2+ TCR recognizes phosphoantigens such as (E)–4-hydroxy-3-methyl-but-2-enyl pyrophosphate (HMB-PP) and isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), the intermediate metabolites of the 2-C-methyl-D-erythritol 4-phosphate (MEP) pathway in many bacteria and the mevalonate pathway in mammalian cells, respectively (Tanaka et al., 1995; Gu et al., 2014; Simões et al., 2018; Tyler et al., 2015; Hintz et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 1995; Gu et al., 2014; Simões et al., 2018; Tyler et al., 2015; Hintz et al., 2001.

claims.claim: The phosphoantigens are identified by Vδ2 T cells in the context of Butyrophilin 2A1 and 3A1 molecules.
claims.source: The phosphoantigens are identified by Vδ2 T cells in the context of Butyrophilin 2A1 and 3A1 molecules (Laplagne et al., 2021; Cano et al., 2021; Fulford et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Laplagne et al., 2021; Cano et al., 2021; Fulford et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Numerous in vivo and in vitro studies point to the involvement of Vδ2 T cells in the defense against malignant cells and various pathogens.
claims.source: Numerous in vivo and in vitro studies point to the involvement of Vδ2 T cells in the defense against malignant cells (Schönefeldt et al., 2021) and various pathogens such as M. tuberculosis (Dieli et al., 2000; Chen, 2016), Plasmodium falciparum (Hernández-Castañeda et al., 2020; Howard et al., 2018; Junqueira et al., 2021), Listeria monocytogenes (Ryan-Payseur et al., 2012), Brucella suis (Bessoles et al., 2011; Oliaro et al., 2005), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (He et al., 2013; Poccia et al., 1999), influenza virus (Qin et al., 2011; Qin et al., 2009), hepatitis C virus (Cimini et al., 2018), severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus SARS-CoV (Poccia et al., 2006), and possibly many others (Gay et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to various studies.

claims.claim: Upon activation, Vδ2 T cells produce mainly TNF and IFN-γ, but are also able to secrete IL-17 or IL-4 in certain conditions.
claims.source: Upon activation, Vδ2 T cells produce mainly TNF and IFN-γ, but are also able to secrete IL-17 (Ness-Schwickerath et al., 2010) or IL-4 (Wesch et al., 2001) in certain conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ness-Schwickerath et al., 2010; Wesch et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Vδ2 T cells directly kill target cells by cytotoxic activity, phagocytosis, induction of apoptosis via Fas-Fas ligand interactions, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC), or by mobilizing other immune cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, they directly kill target cells by cytotoxic activity (Dieli et al., 2000; Tokuyama et al., 2008), phagocytosis (Junqueira et al., 2021), induction of apoptosis via Fas-Fas ligand interactions (Li et al., 2011), antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) (Gertner-Dardenne et al., 2009; Capietto et al., 2011; Tokuyama et al., 2008) or by mobilizing other immune cells (Hu et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to various studies.

claims.claim: Professional antigen-presenting capabilities and B cell helper function were described in Vδ2 T cells.
claims.source: For example, professional antigen-presenting capabilities (Junqueira et al., 2021; Brandes et al., 2005) and B cell helper function (Caccamo et al., 2006) were also described in Vδ2 T cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Junqueira et al., 2021; Brandes et al., 2005; Caccamo et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cells have been described in non-human primates and alpacas but no such cell population exists in mice.
claims.source: Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cells have also been described in non-human primates (Kazen and Adams, 2011; Wang et al., 2003) and alpacas (Fichtner et al., 2020b) but no such cell population exists in mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kazen and Adams, 2011; Wang et al., 2003; Fichtner et al., 2020b.

claims.claim: Vδ1 T cells are the second most abundant γδ T cell population in the human peripheral blood and are enriched at barrier tissues.
claims.source: The second most abundant γδ T cell population in the human peripheral blood are Vδ1 T cells, which are enriched at barrier tissues (Qu et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Qu et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The Vδ1 chain is known to pair with various γ chains, including γ2, γ3, γ4, γ5, and γ8.
claims.source: The Vδ1 chain is known to pair with various γ chains, including γ2, γ3, γ4, γ5, and γ8.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of γδ T cell biology.

claims.claim: Vδ1 T cells are largely found in the skin, gut, liver, spleen, lung, and bone marrow.
claims.source: The cells are largely found in the skin, gut, liver, spleen, lung, and bone marrow and recognize CD1 lipid-presenting molecules via their TCR (Spada et al., 2000) as well as stress-inducible MICA and MICB molecules upon tumor transformation or viral infection (Groh et al., 1998; Groh et al., 1999), although this recognition is likely not mediated by the TCR (Bauer et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Spada et al., 2000; Groh et al., 1998; Groh et al., 1999; Bauer et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Vδ1 T cells recognize CD1 lipid-presenting molecules via their TCR.
claims.source: The cells are largely found in the skin, gut, liver, spleen, lung, and bone marrow and recognize CD1 lipid-presenting molecules via their TCR (Spada et al., 2000) as well as stress-inducible MICA and MICB molecules upon tumor transformation or viral infection (Groh et al., 1998; Groh et al., 1999), although this recognition is likely not mediated by the TCR (Bauer et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spada et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Vδ1 T cells recognize stress-inducible MICA and MICB molecules upon tumor transformation or viral infection, although this recognition is likely not mediated by the TCR.
claims.source: The cells are largely found in the skin, gut, liver, spleen, lung, and bone marrow and recognize CD1 lipid-presenting molecules via their TCR (Spada et al., 2000) as well as stress-inducible MICA and MICB molecules upon tumor transformation or viral infection (Groh et al., 1998; Groh et al., 1999), although this recognition is likely not mediated by the TCR (Bauer et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Groh et al., 1998; Groh et al., 1999; Bauer et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Functionally, Vδ1 T cells resemble cytotoxic, Th1-like phenotypes characterized by IFN-γ expression.
claims.source: Functionally, they resemble cytotoxic, Th1-like phenotypes characterized by IFN-γ expression (Deusch et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deusch et al., 1991.

claims.claim: Vδ1 T cells are involved in killing various epithelial tumors.
claims.source: Apart from killing various epithelial tumors (Maeurer et al., 1996), Vδ1 T cells are also involved in tissue homeostasis and wound healing by producing insulin-like growth factor-1 (Toulon et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maeurer et al., 1996; Toulon et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Vδ1 T cells are involved in tissue homeostasis and wound healing by producing insulin-like growth factor-1.
claims.source: Apart from killing various epithelial tumors (Maeurer et al., 1996), Vδ1 T cells are also involved in tissue homeostasis and wound healing by producing insulin-like growth factor-1 (Toulon et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Toulon et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and possibly HIV and P. falciparum drive TCR-dependent expansion of Vδ1 T cells.
claims.source: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) and possibly HIV and P. falciparum drive TCR-dependent expansion of Vδ1 T cells (Hviid et al., 2001; De Maria et al., 1992; Vermijlen et al., 2010; Déchanet et al., 1999; McMurray et al., 2022; Ho et al., 1994; Worku et al., 2003; von Borstel et al., 2021), yet the role of Vδ1 T cells in the defense against these pathogens is not clear.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations but notes uncertainty about functional role.

claims.claim: Vδ1 T cells are considered to have an adaptive immune character based on clonal expansion observed upon viral and parasitic infections.
claims.source: Based on clonal expansion of Vδ1 T cells observed upon viral and parasitic infections and consequent generation of a long-lived, TCR-focused effector T cell population, they are considered to have an adaptive immune character (von Borstel et al., 2021; Davey et al., 2017; Ravens et al., 2017; McMurray et al., 2022; Hunter et al., 2018; Rutishauser et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Liver-resident Vδ2- T cells, including Vδ1 T cells, have been shown to be polyfunctional and responsive to both TCR and innate stimuli.
claims.source: Yet, liver-resident Vδ2- T cells, including Vδ1 T cells, have been shown to be polyfunctional and responsive to both TCR and innate stimuli (Hunter et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hunter et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Vδ3 T cells are a minor human γδ T cell population in peripheral blood but are mainly located in the liver, gut, bone marrow, and lymph nodes.
claims.source: Vδ3 T cells are a minor human γδ T cell population in peripheral blood but are mainly located in the liver, gut, bone marrow, and lymph nodes and significantly expand in certain pathological conditions (Hunter et al., 2018; Dunne et al., 2013; Kenna et al., 2004; Kabelitz et al., 1997; Falk et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hunter et al., 2018; Dunne et al., 2013; Kenna et al., 2004; Kabelitz et al., 1997; Falk et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Vδ3 T cells recognize the stress-related molecules CD1d and annexin-A2 (ANX).
claims.source: They recognize the stress-related molecules CD1d and annexin-A2 (ANX) (Mangan et al., 2013; Marlin et al., 2017) and produce mainly TNF (Petrasca et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mangan et al., 2013; Marlin et al., 2017; Petrasca et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Vδ3 T cells have been shown to induce dendritic cell (DC) maturation to cytokine-producing APCs.
claims.source: Although there are limited reports on the function of Vδ3 T cells, they have been shown to induce dendritic cell (DC) maturation to cytokine-producing APCs (Mangan et al., 2013) and B cell maturation to IgM-secreting cells (Petrasca et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mangan et al., 2013; Petrasca et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Vδ5 T cells are a little-known subset recognizing stressed cells via the endothelial protein C receptor (EPRC).
claims.source: Vδ5 T cells are a little-known subset recognizing stressed cells via the endothelial protein C receptor (EPRC), yet their functions remain largely elusive (Willcox et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Willcox et al., 2012.

claims.claim: A more diverse δ chain repertoire exists in peripheral blood and liver, including Vδ4, Vδ6, Vδ7, and Vδ8.
claims.source: Recent findings indicate that a more diverse δ chain repertoire exists, particularly in peripheral blood and liver, including Vδ4, Vδ6, Vδ7, and Vδ8 (Hunter et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2014; Christopoulos et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hunter et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2014; Christopoulos et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Vγ1, Vγ2, Vγ3, Vγ4, Vγ5, Vγ6, and Vγ7 subsets have been identified in mice.
claims.source: Vγ1, Vγ2, Vγ3, Vγ4, Vγ5, Vγ6, and Vγ7 subsets have been identified in mice so far (Heilig and Tonegawa's nomenclature [Heilig and Tonegawa, 1986]) adopted in this review (McMurray et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heilig and Tonegawa, 1986; McMurray et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The γ chains predominantly found in mouse γδ TCRs are Vγ1 and Vγ4, which pair with a variety of delta chains.
claims.source: The γ chains predominantly found in mouse γδ TCRs are Vγ1 and Vγ4, which pair with a variety of delta chains (He et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Vγ1 and Vγ4 T cells are found in peripheral blood, secondary lymphoid organs, liver, and lung.
claims.source: Vγ1 and Vγ4 T cells are found in peripheral blood, secondary lymphoid organs, liver, and lung (He et al., 2010; Pereira et al., 1995; Qi et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to He et al., 2010; Pereira et al., 1995; Qi et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Resident Vγ1 T cells in lymphoid tissues support B cell differentiation and antibody production upon vaccination or infection.
claims.source: Resident Vγ1 T cells in lymphoid tissues support B cell differentiation and antibody production upon vaccination or infection (Ullrich et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2009), while in the lung, they promote allergic airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) by synergizing with invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells (Jin et al., 2009; Hahn et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ullrich et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2009; Hahn et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Vγ1 T cells have been shown to protect from Coxsackievirus B3 infection-induced myocarditis by promoting Th2 responses.
claims.source: They have also been shown to protect from Coxsackievirus B3 infection-induced myocarditis by promoting Th2 responses (Huber et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huber et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Vγ4 T cells present in the dermis primarily produce IL-17A during mycobacterial infection to promote neutrophil infiltration to the skin.
claims.source: Vγ4 T cells present in the dermis primarily produce IL-17A during mycobacterial infection to further promote neutrophil infiltration to the skin (Sumaria et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sumaria et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Mucosal and hepatic Vγ4 T cells play an important role in protecting mice from L. monocytogenes infection by producing IFN-γ and IL17A and collaborating with αβ T cells.
claims.source: Mucosal and hepatic Vγ4 T cells play an important role in protecting the mice from L. monocytogenes infection by producing IFN-γ and IL17A and collaborating with αβ T cells (Sheridan et al., 2013; Hamada et al., 2008b; Khairallah et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sheridan et al., 2013; Hamada et al., 2008b; Khairallah et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Vγ1 and Vγ4 T cells have opposing roles in selected disease models.
claims.source: It is also interesting to note that Vγ1 and Vγ4 T cells are shown to have opposing roles in selected disease models (Hahn et al., 2004; Huber et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2004; Huber et al., 2000.

claims.claim: AHR is promoted by Vγ1 cells but suppressed by Vγ4 cells in a mouse asthma model.
claims.source: For example, as mentioned, AHR is promoted by Vγ1 cells but suppressed by Vγ4 cells in a mouse asthma model (Hahn et al., 2004), while the susceptibility to Coxsackievirus B3-induced myocarditis is suppressed by Vγ1 cells but promoted by Vγ4 cells (Huber et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2004; Huber et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Vγ6 T cells are present in the mouse lung.
claims.source: Apart from Vγ1 and Vγ4, Vγ6 T cells are also present in the mouse lung (Sim et al., 1994; Hayes et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sim et al., 1994; Hayes et al., 1996.

claims.claim: Upon infection, Vγ1, Vγ4, and Vγ6 T cells in the lung proliferate and secrete distinct chemokines and cytokines to recruit other immune cells, mainly neutrophils.
claims.source: Upon infection, all these three subsets proliferate and secrete distinct chemokines and cytokines, such as CXCL2 and TNF, to recruit other immune cells, mainly neutrophils (Nakasone et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nakasone et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Vγ6 T cells are broadly distributed in various tissues, including the peritoneal cavity, reproductive tract, tongue, placenta/decidua, dermis, gingiva, nasal epithelium and tendon-to-bone attachment sites.
claims.source: The localization of Vγ6 T cells is not limited to the lung; they are broadly distributed in various tissues, including the peritoneal cavity (O'Brien et al., 2010), reproductive tract (Itohara et al., 1990), tongue (Itohara et al., 1990), placenta/decidua (Heyborne et al., 1992; Pinget et al., 2016), dermis (Cai et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2019), gingiva (Wilharm et al., 2019), nasal epithelium (Kim et al., 2008) and tendon-to-bone attachment sites (Reinhardt et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to various studies.

claims.claim: Vγ6 T cells have been found to expand in response to a variety of bacteria and in several disease models.
claims.source: These cells have been found to expand in response to a variety of bacteria (e.g., Listeria [Sheridan et al., 2013; Hamada et al., 2008a; Ikebe et al., 2001], Escherichia coli [Shibata et al., 2007], Bacillus subtilis [Simonian et al., 2006], M. tuberculosis [Umemura et al., 2016], Streptococcus pneumoniae [Paget et al., 2015], and Staphylococcus aureus [Hamada et al., 2008b; Marchitto et al., 2019]) and in several disease models, including pulmonary fibrosis (Simonian et al., 2009), nephritis (Wu et al., 2004), and testicular inflammation (Mukasa et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to various studies.

claims.claim: Vγ5 T cells are the predominant population in the epidermis of rodent skin and are also called dendritic epidermal T cells (DETC).
claims.source: Vγ5 T cells are the predominant population in the epidermis of rodent skin, where they maintain their homeostatic density throughout life by self-renewal capacity. They are also called dendritic epidermal T cells (DETC) and have unique roles in wound healing and immune surveillance (Sutoh et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sutoh et al., 2018.

claims.claim: In stressed skin, DETCs are activated, resulting in elevated IFN-γ and IL-17 production as well as cytotoxic properties.
claims.source: In stressed skin, DETCs are activated, resulting in elevated IFN-γ and IL-17 production as well as cytotoxic properties (Nielsen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nielsen et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The Vγ7 subset is most abundant in the epithelial layer of the gut, playing essential roles in maintaining intestinal homeostasis and responding to pathogens or tissue damage.
claims.source: Lastly, the Vγ7 subset is most abundant in the epithelial layer of the gut, playing essential roles in maintaining intestinal homeostasis and responding to pathogens or tissue damage by producing mainly IFN-γ together with a wide range of other cytokines such as TNF, TGF-β, IL-10, IL-13, and displaying high cytotoxic potential (Li et al., 2023b; Di Marco Barros et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2023b; Di Marco Barros et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Vγ7 T cells play different roles in the different stages of colitis: a pathogenic role in the early stage but a protective role in the later stage.
claims.source: Interestingly, it has been shown that these cells play different roles in the different stages of colitis: a pathogenic role in the early stage but a protective role in the later stage (Kühl et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kühl et al., 2007.

claims.claim: There is a significant population of Vγ6 T cells in the gut lamina propria that predominantly produces IL-17 and IL-22 to limit bacterial invasion and intestinal inflammation.
claims.source: There is also a significant population of Vγ6 T cells in the gut lamina propria that predominantly produces IL-17 and IL-22 to limit bacterial invasion and intestinal inflammation (Rampoldi and Prinz, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rampoldi and Prinz, 2022.

claims.claim: γδ T cells are found in all jawed vertebrates.
claims.source: γδ T cells are found in all jawed vertebrates (Holderness et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holderness et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Artiodactyls, specifically cattle and swine, have relatively high frequencies of γδ T cells in blood, accounting for up to 60% of circulating lymphocytes, especially in young animals.
claims.source: Artiodactyls, specifically cattle and swine, have relatively high frequencies of γδ T cells in blood, accounting for up to 60% of circulating lymphocytes, especially in young animals (Talker et al., 2013; Guzman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Talker et al., 2013; Guzman et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Cattle γδ T cells are identified as WC1−, WC1.1+, and WC1.2+ subsets and are involved in responses to severe infections such as foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV).
claims.source: Cattle γδ T cells are identified as WC1−, WC1.1+, and a WC1.2+ subsets and are involved in responses to severe infections such as that caused by foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) (Wilharm et al., 2019; Toka et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wilharm et al., 2019; Toka et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Cattle γδ T cells display a great proliferative response in the peripheral blood of animals infected with bovine herpesvirus type I and bovine diarrhea virus infections.
claims.source: They display a great proliferative response in the peripheral blood of animals infected with bovine herpesvirus type I and bovine diarrhea virus infections (Silflow et al., 2005; Amadori et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Silflow et al., 2005; Amadori et al., 1995.

claims.claim: WC1.2+ γδ T cell clones in cattle proliferate and secrete IFN-γ in response to Anaplasma marginale.
claims.source: While WC1.2+ γδ T cell clones in cattle proliferate and secrete IFN-γ in response to Anaplasma marginale (Lahmers et al., 2006; Lahmers et al., 2005), M. tuberculosis elicits preferential activation of the WC1.1+γδ T cell subset (Bhat et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lahmers et al., 2006; Lahmers et al., 2005; Bhat et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Although γδ T cells strongly proliferate upon mycobacterial stimulation ex vivo in cattle, they release minute amounts of IFN-γ.
claims.source: Although γδ T cells strongly proliferate upon mycobacterial stimulation ex vivo, they release minute amounts of IFN-γ (Smyth et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smyth et al., 2001.

claims.claim: In swine, γδ T cells represent an important source of IFN-γ and IL-17 production, express cytotoxic activity and orchestrate both innate and adaptive immune responses upon infection with reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus infection.
claims.source: In swine, γδ T cells represent an important source of IFN-γ and IL-17 production, express cytotoxic activity and orchestrate both innate and adaptive immune responses upon infection with reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus infection (Le Page et al., 2022; Olin et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Le Page et al., 2022; Olin et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Deletion of γδ T cells does not alter the structure of immune organs or the health of conventionally housed pigs but may reduce responses to live-attenuated vaccines.
claims.source: Deletion of γδ T cells does not alter the structure of immune organs or the health of conventionally housed pigs but may reduce responses to live-attenuated vaccines (Petersen et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Petersen et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Birds, such as chickens, have a high frequency of γδ T cells in the intestinal mucosa.
claims.source: Birds, such as chickens, have a high frequency of γδ T cells in the intestinal mucosa.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: During infection with Eimeria acervulina, an early increase of local intestinal γδ T cells has been observed in chickens, reflecting their role in early host defense.
claims.source: During infection with Eimeria acervulina, an early increase of local intestinal γδ T cells has been observed, reflecting their role in early host defense (Choi and Lillehoj, 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Choi and Lillehoj, 2000.

claims.claim: The absence of γδ T cells leaves chicken health under conventional breeding unaltered.
claims.source: While the absence of γδ T leaves chicken health under conventional breeding unaltered (von Heyl et al., 2023), it does cause susceptibility to an avian oncogenic alphaherpesvirus (Sabsabi et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to von Heyl et al., 2023; Sabsabi et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Certain vertebrates, such as squamate reptiles, lost γδ T cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, certain vertebrates, such as squamate reptiles, are unique in that they lost γδ T cells (Morrissey et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morrissey et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The lack of TCRγ and TCRδ transcripts in snakes and lizards seems to be due to large genome deletions in the absence of compensatory changes in the conventional T cell genes.
claims.source: The lack of TCRγ and TCRδ transcripts seems to be due to large genome deletions in the absence of compensatory changes in the conventional T cell genes in snakes and lizards.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on genomic analysis.

claims.claim: Immune memory responses of γδ T cells have been documented in humans, cattle and mice.
claims.source: Immune memory responses of γδ T cells have been documented in humans, cattle and mice (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim references Table 1 which contains data on immune memory responses.

claims.claim: Hoft et al. observed a drastic expansion of γδ T cells after in vitro stimulation with Mycobacterium tuberculosis of PBMCs from BCG-vaccinated individuals compared to non-vaccinated donors.
claims.source: Already in the early 80s, Hoft et al. observed a drastic expansion of γδ T cells after the in vitro stimulation with Mycobacterium tuberculosis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from BCG-vaccinated individuals compared to the non-vaccinated donors or placebo recipients (Hoft et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hoft et al., 1998.

claims.claim: The highly reactive γδ T cells after BCG vaccination were mainly Vδ2 T cell subsets, most likely Vγ9Vδ2 T cell subset.
claims.source: The highly reactive γδ T cells were mainly Vδ2 T cell subsets, most likely Vγ9Vδ2 T cell subset (Kabelitz et al., 1991), and their enhanced responsiveness to M. tuberculosis after BCG vaccination was shown to be independent of the helper function of CD4 T cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kabelitz et al., 1991.

claims.claim: The frequencies of IFN-γ-producing cells upon in vitro re-stimulation were increased among γδ T cells from BCG-vaccinated individuals.
claims.source: Apart from greater expansion, the frequencies of IFN-γ-producing cells upon in vitro re-stimulation were also increased among γδ T cells from BCG-vaccinated individuals (Suliman et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suliman et al., 2016.

claims.claim: BCG-vaccinated macaques displayed an enhanced expansion of peripheral blood and pulmonary Vδ2 T cells upon reinfection with BCG or M. tuberculosis compared to unvaccinated animals.
claims.source: Similar observations were made in BCG-vaccinated macaques, which displayed an enhanced expansion of peripheral blood and pulmonary Vδ2 T cells upon reinfection with BCG or M. tuberculosis compared to unvaccinated animals (Shen et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shen et al., 2002; Lai et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Enhanced expansion of Vδ2 T cells in BCG-vaccinated macaques coincided with improved microbial clearance, suggesting a protective role of the Vδ2 T cell recall responses.
claims.source: This coincided with improved microbial clearance, suggesting a protective role of the Vδ2 T cell recall responses, which were shown to be specific to the mycobacterial antigens.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on correlation between Vδ2 T cell expansion and microbial clearance.

claims.claim: Neither BCG vaccination of infants nor re-vaccination of adults induced T cell memory phenotype in γδ T cells defined by the expression of CD45RA and CCR7 surface molecules.

claims.source: Furthermore, the inflamed sites were associated with heightened neutrophil recruitment and more rapid ear thickening upon re-challenge, which was dependent on Vγ4+Vδ4+ T cell presence, indicating that γδ T cell immune memory responses orchestrate other cells of the immune system (Hartwig et al., 2015).

claims.source: Interestingly, intestinal memory Vγ4+Vδ1+ T cells generated in response to food-borne L. monocytogenes infection seem to be reactive to unrelated bacteria such as Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and Citrobacter rodentium when rechallenged ex vivo and to Yersinia pseudotuberculosis when rechallenged in vivo (Khairallah et al., 2022).

claims.source: Importantly, chromatin accessibility analysis further revealed increased promoter accessibility of certain innate immunity-related genes in the trained bovine γδ T cells, which is consistent with the common phenotype of epigenetic reprogramming in trained immunity.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that immune memory, historically attributed exclusively to adaptive immunity, is now recognized in innate immune cells through a phenomenon termed 'trained immunity'.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C3, C8, C9, and C22 collectively establish the historical context (C1, C22) and recent paradigm shift (C2, C8, C9) regarding immune memory. These claims are well-supported by citations to established literature (C2, C8, C9) and represent accepted knowledge in the field (C3).

results.result: γδ T cells possess unique features of both adaptive and innate immunity, with their memory responses originally characterized as adaptive but growing evidence showing they can also mount antigen-independent memory responses resembling trained immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 establish the dual nature of γδ T cells and the evolution of understanding about their memory responses. These claims are supported by citations to published research (C7) and represent the central thesis of the review. The characterization is consistent with established immunological knowledge.

results.result: Innate immunity, comprising phagocytes that use germline-encoded pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) to recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), emerged as the first antimicrobial defense strategy and initiates adaptive immune responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C16 describe fundamental principles of innate immunity that are well-established in immunology. These claims are supported by citations to authoritative sources (C10, C14, C15) and represent textbook knowledge about innate immune system function.

results.result: Adaptive immune cells (B and T cells) are activated later in infection in an antigen-specific manner through highly diverse BCRs and TCRs generated by somatic recombination, with memory B and T cells persisting to enable faster responses upon rechallenge.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C24 describe fundamental principles of adaptive immunity that are well-established. The claims about somatic recombination (C19) and memory cell persistence (C23, C24) are supported by citations to established literature and represent textbook immunology.

results.result: Memory B and T cells respond faster and more effectively than naïve cells due to epigenetic reprogramming involving redistribution of DNA methylation and histone modifications that create a poised chromatin state, along with metabolic reprogramming including increased mitochondrial capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C31 describe the molecular mechanisms underlying adaptive immune memory. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research (C25, C26, C27, C29, C30) and represent established understanding of memory T cell biology.

results.result: Innate immune memory (trained immunity) is not antigen-specific and was originally discovered in monocytes/macrophages responding to C. albicans and BCG. Trained cells undergo metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming including augmented glycolysis, OXPHOS, and accumulation of activating histone modifications at immune response genes, with induction occurring at the level of myeloid progenitors in bone marrow.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C40 comprehensively describe trained immunity mechanisms. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research (C33, C35, C36, C37, C38, C39, C40) and represent established understanding of trained immunity. The distinction from adaptive memory (C32) is clearly articulated.

results.result: Trained immunity is hypothesized to underlie heterologous protection from live attenuated vaccines (BCG, OPV, MMR) and can enhance host defense but may also lead to maladaptive inflammatory responses in conditions like gout, rheumatoid arthritis, and atherosclerosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 describe the functional implications of trained immunity. C41 is appropriately characterized as a hypothesis with citation support (Benn et al., 2013). C42-C43 are supported by citations to research linking trained immunity to inflammatory diseases. The dual nature (beneficial and detrimental) is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: γδ T cells are a distinct T cell subset with unique attributes including rapid tissue protection, homeostasis maintenance, and cancer detection. Their TCR consists of gamma and delta chains that recognize nonpeptidic ligands in an MHC-independent manner, with some γδ TCRs being polyspecific.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C51 provide foundational characterization of γδ T cells. These claims are well-supported by citations to established research (C45, C46, C47, C50) and represent accepted knowledge about γδ T cell biology. The distinction from αβ T cells is clearly articulated.

results.result: γδ T cells express innate immune receptors including NKG2C, NKG2D, TLRs (TLR2, TLR3, TLR6), NOD2, and STING receptors that recognize stress molecules and PAMPs, with ligand stimulation co-stimulating TCR-activated cells to enhance cytokine and chemokine production.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 describe the innate immune receptor repertoire of γδ T cells. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research (C52, C53, C54, C55, C56, C57) demonstrating the expression and function of various innate receptors on γδ T cells.

results.result: γδ TCR assembly requires VDJ recombination during thymic development with diversity increased by random nucleotide addition/deletion at junction sites, generating exceptionally long and flexible CDR3 loops that enable recognition of diverse pathogens and non-peptide ligands, though the diversity potential is not fully realized.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 describe γδ TCR diversity generation. These claims are well-supported by citations to established research (C59, C60, C61, C63, C64). The structural basis for broad ligand recognition (C62) is a reasonable inference from the described CDR3 properties.

results.result: During thymic development, TRG locus rearrangement precedes TRB and is followed by TRD recombination. Upon successful VDJ rearrangement of both chains, cells commit to the γδ lineage and undergo 'γδ selection', though whether this is ligand-dependent remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 describe γδ T cell development. C65-C66 are supported by citations to established research (C66). C67 appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about ligand-dependence with supporting citations, demonstrating appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The main human γδ T cell subsets are Vδ1, Vδ2, Vδ3, and Vδ5, with Vδ2 being best characterized. Vδ2 predominantly pairs with γ9 (Vγ9+Vδ2+) comprising up to 90% of peripheral blood γδ T cells, with Vγ9+Vδ2+ bearing innate immunity characteristics while Vγ9-Vδ2+ has adaptive immune character.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 describe human γδ T cell subset classification. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to established research (C68, C70, C71, C72). The functional distinction between Vγ9+ and Vγ9- subsets (C72) is appropriately cited.

results.result: Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cells recognize phosphoantigens (HMB-PP, IPP) in the context of Butyrophilin molecules and are involved in defense against malignant cells and various pathogens. Upon activation, they produce TNF and IFN-γ, kill targets through multiple mechanisms, and can function as APCs and B cell helpers. These cells exist in non-human primates and alpacas but not mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C80 comprehensively describe Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cell function. These claims are extensively supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research covering antigen recognition (C73, C74, C75), pathogen defense (C76), effector functions (C77, C78), and APC capabilities (C79). Species distribution (C80) is appropriately cited.

results.result: Vδ1 T cells are the second most abundant γδ T cell population in human peripheral blood, enriched at barrier tissues. They pair with various γ chains, recognize CD1 lipid molecules and stress-inducible MICA/MICB, display Th1-like cytotoxic phenotypes, and are involved in tumor killing and tissue homeostasis. CMV, HIV, and P. falciparum drive TCR-dependent expansion, and they are considered to have adaptive immune character, though liver-resident Vδ1 cells respond to both TCR and innate stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C91 comprehensively describe Vδ1 T cell biology. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research covering tissue distribution (C81, C83), antigen recognition (C84, C85), function (C86, C87, C88), pathogen responses (C89, C90), and dual responsiveness (C91). The uncertainty about pathogen defense role (C89) is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Vδ3 T cells are a minor population in peripheral blood but located in liver, gut, bone marrow, and lymph nodes, recognizing CD1d and annexin-A2 and producing TNF. They induce DC and B cell maturation. Vδ5 T cells recognize stressed cells via EPRC but remain poorly characterized. A more diverse δ chain repertoire (Vδ4, Vδ6, Vδ7, Vδ8) exists in peripheral blood and liver.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 describe less abundant human γδ T cell subsets. These claims are appropriately supported by citations (C92, C93, C94, C95, C96). The acknowledgment of limited knowledge about Vδ5 cells (C95) and detection of rare subsets only in pathological conditions (C96) demonstrates appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Mouse γδ T cells include Vγ1-7 subsets, with Vγ1 and Vγ4 being predominant. Vγ1 cells in lymphoid tissues support B cell responses and promote AHR in lung, while protecting from Coxsackievirus B3 myocarditis. Vγ4 cells produce IL-17A during mycobacterial infection and protect from L. monocytogenes. Vγ1 and Vγ4 cells have opposing roles in some disease models.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C105 describe mouse γδ T cell subsets and functions. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research (C97, C98, C99, C100, C101, C102, C103, C104, C105). The observation of opposing roles in disease models (C104, C105) is appropriately documented with citations.

results.result: Vγ6 T cells are present in mouse lung and broadly distributed in various tissues including peritoneal cavity, reproductive tract, dermis, and other sites. Upon infection, Vγ1, Vγ4, and Vγ6 cells proliferate and secrete chemokines/cytokines to recruit neutrophils. Vγ6 cells expand in response to various bacteria and in disease models.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 describe Vγ6 T cell distribution and function. These claims are extensively supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research covering tissue localization (C106, C108), infection responses (C107), and bacterial/disease model responses (C109).

results.result: Vγ5 T cells (DETCs) are predominant in rodent epidermis with self-renewal capacity and roles in wound healing and immune surveillance, producing IFN-γ and IL-17 when activated. Vγ7 cells are most abundant in gut epithelium, maintaining intestinal homeostasis and responding to pathogens with different roles in early vs. late colitis. Vγ6 cells in gut lamina propria produce IL-17 and IL-22 to limit bacterial invasion.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C114 describe tissue-resident mouse γδ T cell subsets. These claims are well-supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C110, C111, C112, C113, C114). The stage-specific roles in colitis (C113) represent an important functional observation appropriately cited.

results.result: γδ T cells are found in all jawed vertebrates. Cattle and swine have high frequencies (up to 60% of lymphocytes). Cattle γδ T cells (WC1−, WC1.1+, WC1.2+ subsets) respond to FMDV and other infections, with subset-specific responses to different pathogens. Swine γδ T cells produce IFN-γ and IL-17, with deletion not affecting health under conventional housing but potentially reducing vaccine responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C122 describe γδ T cells in livestock species. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research (C115, C116, C117, C118, C119, C120, C121, C122). The functional observations and deletion studies are appropriately documented.

results.result: Chickens have high frequencies of γδ T cells in intestinal mucosa that increase during Eimeria acervulina infection. Absence of γδ T cells doesn't affect health under conventional breeding but causes susceptibility to avian alphaherpesvirus. Squamate reptiles uniquely lost γδ T cells due to large genome deletions.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 describe γδ T cells in birds and reptiles. These claims are supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C124, C125, C126). The genomic basis for γδ T cell loss in reptiles (C127) is presented as an inference, which is appropriate given the evidence.

results.result: BCG vaccination induces adaptive immune memory in human and primate Vδ2 T cells, characterized by drastic expansion upon M. tuberculosis stimulation, increased IFN-γ production, and enhanced responsiveness independent of CD4 T cell help. BCG-vaccinated macaques showed enhanced Vδ2 T cell expansion in blood and lung upon reinfection, coinciding with improved microbial clearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C133 describe adaptive memory responses of Vδ2 T cells to BCG vaccination. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research (C129, C130, C131, C132). The correlation between enhanced responses and microbial clearance (C133) is appropriately characterized as an inference based on observed correlation.

results.result: BCG vaccination of infants or adults did not induce classical T cell memory phenotype (CD45RA-CCR7-) in γδ T cells. Instead, frequencies of terminally differentiated effector cells increased while effector memory cells decreased, accompanied by increased naïve cell frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 describe unexpected phenotypic changes after BCG vaccination. These claims are well-supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C134, C135) and represent an important observation that challenges simple classification of γδ T cell memory as purely adaptive.

results.result: Vδ2 T cells mount pathogen-specific recall responses to L. monocytogenes in macaques, with enhanced proliferation, effector function, and enrichment in lung and intestinal mucosa upon secondary challenge. The antigen is most likely HMBPP, though in vitro HMBPP exposure results in polyclonal proliferation, questioning the adaptive character of Vγ9Vδ2 responses to phosphoantigens.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C141 describe L. monocytogenes memory responses. While C136-C139 are supported by citations and experimental data, C141 presents contradictory evidence showing polyclonal rather than clonal responses to phosphoantigens. This contradiction raises questions about whether these responses are truly adaptive or have innate-like features, warranting an UNCERTAIN evaluation.

results.result: Vδ2 T cells respond to P. falciparum sporozoite vaccine, with their expansion being the best correlate of protection. Vδ1 T cell frequencies increase after repeated malaria exposure, negatively correlating with symptom severity. Vδ1 cells from naïve individuals are unresponsive to parasite extracts but gain proliferative responses after exposure, differentiating toward cytotoxic effector phenotype. Malaria causes clonal expansion of Vδ2- cells with TCR repertoire focusing, while Vδ2+ clonotypes remain stable.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C151 comprehensively describe γδ T cell responses to malaria. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to peer-reviewed research (C142, C143, C145, C151) and experimental observations (C146, C147, C148, C149, C150). The distinction between Vδ1 and Vδ2 responses represents an important finding about subset-specific memory characteristics.

results.result: γδ T cells contribute to long-term immune memory against P. falciparum in CHMI trials. The parasite activated and expanded peripheral blood γδ T cells, boosted effector memory cell frequencies, and increased IFN-γ-producing cells after secondary exposure, with γδ T cells being the main IFN-γ producers during recall despite small numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C155 describe γδ T cell memory responses in CHMI trials. These claims are well-supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C152, C153, C155) and experimental observations (C154). The observation that γδ T cells are main IFN-γ producers despite low numbers (C155) is particularly notable.

results.result: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine induces memory phenotype in Vδ2 T cells. The first dose had little effect on transcriptome, but the booster caused profound changes including central memory transcriptional signature, increased expansion capacity, and enhanced IFN-γ production upon re-exposure to spike proteins. AP-1 family transcription factors accompanied these changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C160 describe SARS-CoV-2 vaccine-induced memory in Vδ2 T cells. These claims are supported by citation to peer-reviewed research (C156) and experimental observations (C157, C158, C159, C160). The dose-dependent effects and transcriptional changes represent important mechanistic insights.

results.result: Vδ2 T cells respond to vaccinia virus immunization and Mpox virus infection. In macaques, suboptimal priming with vaccinia virus plus cidofovir led to enhanced proliferative response upon subsequent MPV challenge compared to unvaccinated or vaccinated-alone animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C162 describe Vδ2 T cell responses to poxviruses. These claims are supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C161, C162). The observation about suboptimal priming enhancing recall responses is interesting but would benefit from mechanistic explanation.

results.result: CMV seropositive subjects display higher percentages of Vδ1 T cells with restricted TCR repertoire and effector/memory phenotype compared to seronegative individuals. Vδ1 cells from CMV+ patients show enhanced cytotoxic activity upon stimulation with CMV-infected cells. CMV reactivation after immunosuppression causes rapid secondary Vδ1 expansion associated with quicker infection resolution, suggesting CMV drives expansion of memory-like Vδ1 T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C168 describe CMV-driven Vδ1 T cell memory. These claims are well-supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C163, C164, C168) and experimental observations (C165, C166). The association between faster response and infection resolution (C167) is appropriately characterized as correlative.

results.result: Murine intestinal and intrahepatic γδ T cells develop immune memory upon L. monocytogenes infection. Mice orally challenged with L. monocytogenes developed long-lived resident Vγ6 T cells in mesenteric lymph nodes that exhibited more rapid and robust responses upon secondary oral challenge in a pathogen- and site-specific manner. Memory γδ T cells protected via TCR-dependent mechanisms involving IL-17A production and cooperation with conventional T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C172 describe adaptive memory responses in murine γδ T cells. These claims are well-supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C169) and experimental observations (C170, C171). The pathogen and site specificity (C172) is an appropriate inference from the experimental data showing lack of response to intravenous Listeria or oral Salmonella.

results.result: Murine Vγ6 T cells expand vigorously upon S. aureus infection and are retained in draining lymph nodes, peritoneum, and kidney for prolonged periods. Upon reinfection, animals display enhanced expansion, IL-17 production, and reduced bacterial load. Adoptive transfer of S. aureus-experienced γδ T cells improves infection outcomes, with γδ T cell deficiency abrogating this protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C175 describe S. aureus-induced memory in murine γδ T cells. These claims are well-supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C173, C174, C175). The adoptive transfer experiments (C175) provide strong evidence for protective memory function.

results.result: In the absence of conventional T cells and NK cells, murine γδ T cells (mostly Vγ1 and Vγ4) control MCMV infection by restricting viral load. These cells surge in liver, lung, and spleen after infection, displaying effector memory phenotype. Adoptive transfer experiments show mice receiving γδ T cells from MCMV+ donors have higher survival than those receiving cells from MCMV- donors, suggesting γδ T cells play an indispensable role in MCMV re-infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C179 describe MCMV-induced memory in murine γδ T cells. These claims are based on experimental observations (C176, C177, C178). The inference about indispensable role (C179) is appropriately cautious given that killing mechanisms remain undefined, though the adoptive transfer data provide strong support.

results.result: Plasmodium infection causes activation and expansion of murine γδ T cells. Splenocytes from P. chabaudi-infected mice show higher numbers of CD107a+ and IFN-γ-producing γδ T cells upon in vitro rechallenge. γδ effector memory T cells display transcriptional signatures similar to CD8+ memory T cells with upregulation of genes related to cytokines, chemokines, and cytotoxic properties, suggesting murine γδ T cells form pathogen-specific immune memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C183 describe Plasmodium-induced memory in murine γδ T cells. These claims are supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C180, C181) and experimental observations (C182). The inference about pathogen-specific memory (C183) is appropriately based on the transcriptional and functional data.

results.result: Macaques vaccinated with L. monocytogenes-based vaccine showed prolonged Vδ2 T cell expansion dependent on HMBPP production. Upon M. tuberculosis infection, immunized animals had higher numbers of IFN-γ- and perforin-producing Vδ2 T cells in airways, lower pulmonary pathology, and less weight loss. This study demonstrated for the first time pathogen-unspecific but HMBPP-dependent memory responses by primate γδ T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C184-C187 describe cross-protective trained immunity in primate γδ T cells. These claims are supported by citation to peer-reviewed research (C186) and experimental observations (C184, C185). The characterization as 'first demonstration' of pathogen-unspecific memory (C187) represents an important conceptual advance in understanding γδ T cell memory.

results.result: BCG-vaccinated individuals show higher percentages of perforin-producing γδ T cells and increased IFN-γ production upon M. tuberculosis stimulation. Importantly, stimulation with BCG-unrelated pathogens (C. albicans, E. coli, S. aureus) also caused enhanced cytokine production, suggesting trained immunity. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed IFNG upregulation in γδ T cells upon LPS rechallenge 3 months post-vaccination, with cell-cell communication analysis suggesting IFNG-related communication between γδ T cells and monocytes. High interindividual heterogeneity exists in BCG-induced trained immunity capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C193 describe trained immunity induction in human γδ T cells by BCG. These claims are based on experimental observations (C188, C189, C190, C192, C193) and supported by citation regarding heterogeneity (C191). The cross-reactivity to unrelated pathogens (C189, C190) provides strong evidence for trained immunity rather than adaptive memory.

results.result: Stimulation of PBMCs from HSV seropositive patients with HSV-infected cells induced Vδ2 T cell expansion. Vδ2 T cells previously stimulated by PHA or mycobacteria showed increased lysing ability of HSV-infected cells and vaccinia-infected cells (unrelated to HSV). The authors hypothesized that Vδ2 T cell effector function depends on TCR activation by ligands originating from virus-induced modulation of cellular components rather than specific viral antigens.
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C197 describe cross-reactive cytotoxicity by Vδ2 T cells. These claims are supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C194, C196). The hypothesis about TCR ligand origin (C197) is appropriately characterized as speculation. The cross-reactivity against unrelated viruses suggests trained immunity-like features.

results.result: MMR vaccine, known for heterologous protection, induces the biggest transcriptional changes in γδ T cells among PBMC components. Transcriptome and metabolic profiling revealed higher protein synthesis and altered glycolytic capacity/mitochondrial dependency in Vδ2 T cells from vaccinated individuals upon restimulation. TNF and IFN-γ production significantly increased in re-vaccinated volunteers. These changes resemble classical trained immunity phenotype in monocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C198-C202 describe MMR vaccine-induced trained immunity in γδ T cells. These claims are supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C198, C199) and experimental observations (C200, C201). The comparison to monocyte trained immunity (C202) is an appropriate inference based on the metabolic and transcriptional similarities.

results.result: Local skin inflammation with imiquimod (IMQ) established long-lived memory Vγ4+Vδ4+ T cells in mice. After initial IMQ application, IL-17-producing γδ T cells populate dermis and migrate to lymph nodes and distal sites, persisting for months. Upon rechallenge, memory-like cells show rapid expansion, higher IL-17 production, heightened neutrophil recruitment, and increased IL-1R1 expression. Response to mannan was not enhanced, indicating specificity. Recall responses appear TCR-mediated despite IMQ being a TLR-7/8 ligand.
results.evaluation: Claims C203-C210 describe IMQ-induced trained immunity in murine γδ T cells. These claims are well-supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C203, C205, C206, C207, C208, C209, C210). The specificity (C209) and TCR-dependence (C210) are important observations that distinguish this from purely innate responses while showing trained immunity features.

results.result: Intestinal memory Vγ4+Vδ1+ T cells generated in response to L. monocytogenes infection are reactive to unrelated bacteria (S. Typhimurium, C. rodentium, Y. pseudotuberculosis) when rechallenged. This broadly reactive nature suggests potential to induce trained immunity phenotype in these cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C211-C212 describe cross-reactive memory in murine intestinal γδ T cells. C211 is supported by citation to peer-reviewed research. The inference about trained immunity potential (C212) is appropriate given the broad reactivity to unrelated pathogens, which is a hallmark of trained immunity.

results.result: M. bovis infection triggered proliferation of CD27+ γδ T cell memory subset in cattle circulation. BCG-vaccinated cows showed significantly increased IFN-γ-producing γδ T cells upon M. bovis stimulation. γδ T cells from BCG-vaccinated calves show increased IL-6 and TNF production upon stimulation with E. coli, LPS, and Pam3CSK4. Chromatin accessibility analysis revealed increased promoter accessibility of innate immunity-related genes, consistent with epigenetic reprogramming in trained immunity. These observations suggest BCG elicits both adaptive and innate immune memory in bovine γδ T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C213-C217 describe dual memory responses in bovine γδ T cells. These claims are supported by citations to peer-reviewed research (C213, C214, C215) and experimental observations (C216). The epigenetic evidence (C216) provides mechanistic support for trained immunity. The inference about dual memory (C217) is appropriate given the evidence for both pathogen-specific (C213, C214) and cross-reactive (C215) responses.
